Reference / io/decorators

io/decorators#

Readers and writers that wrap others: read ahead, stop at a limit, read one source after another, write to several outputs, or write nowhere.

Version: v1.0.0

Synopsis#

let buffered = BufferedReading(origin: socket, capacity: 8192);
let header = buffered.bytes(32);
let prefix = LimitedReading(origin: file, limit: 1024);
let combined = ChainedReading(origins: parts);
TeeWriting(destinations: outputs).write(packet);
Discarding().write(packet);

Description#

Readers and writers that wrap others: read ahead, stop at a limit, read one source after another, write to several outputs, or write nowhere.

None of them owns or closes what it wraps.

  • BufferedReading reads ahead only when its cache is empty: it asks for the larger of the size asked and its capacity, hands out what was asked and keeps the rest. close() clears only its cache.
  • LimitedReading gives at most limit bytes over all its reads.
  • ChainedReading moves to the next origin when the current one ends with [].
  • TeeWriting takes one snapshot of the source and writes it to each destination in order; the first failure stops the rest, and outputs already written are not undone.
  • Discarding reads source.bytes() once and keeps nothing.

The asynchronous ones wrap AsyncReading and AsyncWriting the same way (#131):

let body = LimitedAsyncReading(origin: socket.input(), limit: length);
let counted = CountingAsyncReading(origin: socket.input());
let patient = TimedAsyncReading(origin: socket.input(), limit: Duration(seconds: 5.rat()), clock: clock);
let output = BufferedAsyncWriting(origin: socket.output(), capacity: 16384);
await output.write(packet);
await output.flush();
  • LimitedAsyncReading gives at most limit bytes over all its reads and never asks origin for more than is left; a zero limit ends at once without reading. Its reads take turns, one at a time in the order they began, so overlapping reads cannot pass the limit together.
  • CountingAsyncReading adds the size of each read it delivers to its count; an end ([]), a failure or a cancelled read adds nothing. Reads go straight to origin, overlapping ones too, and each delivered size is added once. Its count is an Atomic<int>: its own from zero, or one the caller passes and reads; an int does not overflow.
  • TimedAsyncReading limits each read to limit, its clock starting when the read runs, or every read to one deadline fixed beforehand. When time wins, the read is cancelled and its cleanup awaited (Within, Before) before TimedOut is thrown, so nothing goes on reading behind it; a read that settles first keeps its bytes or its failure. A zero limit, or a deadline already passed, leaves only a read already settled. The guarantee is cancellation's: a cleanup that never ends holds the read too.
  • BufferedAsyncWriting gathers writes, in order, up to capacity bytes. A write resolves once its bytes are in the buffer or, when they do not fit, once the buffer and they have gone to origin: a full buffer waits for origin, and nothing reaches origin before flush() or an overflow sends it. Writes and flushes take turns in the order they began. When origin fails or a send is cancelled, part of the bytes may be out and the rest are dropped, never sent twice: the writer is broken and every later write or flush throws BrokenAsyncWriting. It does not flush when it goes; flush() before. A flush hands bytes to origin and promises nothing about a disk or a peer.

None of the asynchronous ones owns or closes origin either.

enum BrokenAsyncWriting#

enum BrokenAsyncWriting is Error = (earlier)

An earlier send of a BufferedAsyncWriting failed or was cancelled: part of its bytes may be out, the rest were dropped, and it writes no more.

earlier

enum ClosedReading#
